content: A honey bee colony may be more than a society of thousands of insects. A new study proposes that the entire colony functions as a single living organism, with its own development, reproductive cycle, and biological lifespan. This perspective could challenge some of the most common practices in modern beekeeping. Researchers Hannes Bonhoff of Lund University and Heikki Helanterä, a professor of evolutionary biology and genomics at the University of Oulu in Finland, argue that a queen and her colony together constitute a superorganism . Rather than treating the queen, 200 to 300 drones, and tens of thousands of workers as separate individuals, their framework considers the colony an animal whose members function much like specialized cells in a body. “We have analyzed what it means for a bee colony to be a single organism, which opens up new insights into the fascinating life of the honey bee,” says Bonhoff. Under this interpretation, a colony develops through stages comparable to those of a mammal, progressing from an embryo and fetus to a juvenile and adult. Bonhoff argues that colonies also undergo biological aging and eventually die after several years. The comparison treats the colony’s development as a whole, rather than focusing on the much shorter lifespans of its individual bees. The superorganism concept is not new, but the researchers apply it to the colony’s life cycle, including how it reproduces and cares for its offspring. This approach raises questions about whether certain behaviors traditionally understood as collective insect activity might instead be viewed as functions of a larger biological individual. Honey bee colonies reproduce through swarming, when the established queen leaves the hive with roughly half the colony to find a new nesting site. A new queen remains in the original hive, where she becomes the reproductive center of the next colony generation. In the researchers’ framework, this process resembles an animal producing offspring and providing extensive parental care. The developing colony inherits an established nest, food resources, shelter, and the support of experienced workers. “When this superorganism reproduces, the offspring are cared for with great dedication by the parent, in some cases even at the cost of the parent’s life,” says Bonhoff. The departing queen and her swarm face the risks of finding and establishing a new home, while the next generation develops in familiar surroundings. Established workers can also provide valuable foraging information through the honey bee dance language, which communicates the locations of food sources. “Parental care therefore goes so far that the offspring inherits the mother’s nest, whilst she herself risks her life by swarming away to settle elsewhere,” says Bonhoff. The proposed framework could have practical implications for managing honey bee populations. Beekeepers commonly replace queens and prevent swarming to maintain productive colonies. However, the researchers suggest that interfering with these natural processes may disrupt the colony’s reproductive and developmental cycle. The study also raises questions about controlling Varroa mites, parasitic arachnids that threaten honey bee populations worldwide. Understanding the colony as an organism with distinct life stages could influence how beekeepers approach parasite management, although the proposed perspective does not itself establish a more effective treatment. “Modern beekeeping methods are based on the idea of keeping the colony young and healthy indefinitely. Our study shows that such interventions fundamentally conflict with the natural reproductive strategy and the ability to cope with parasites,” says Bonhoff. The research originated in Bonhoff’s master’s thesis at Lund University, supervised by Helanterä and Niklas Wahlberg, a professor of systematic biology at Lund. Wahlberg believes the work contributes to understanding how biological individuality can extend beyond a single insect. “The concept itself has been around for a long time, but this is the first time it has been applied in a genuine biological context. It’s fascinating to think that, just as individual cells make up an organism, individual bees with different roles make up the superorganism,” concludes Wahlberg. Reference: “On the life history of the honey bee superorganism” by Hannes A. Bonhoff and Heikki Helanterä, 3 August 2026, Insectes Sociaux . title: Astronomers say they’ve discovered the first green star
content: Astronomers analyzing white dwarf stars have for the first time found a star that would appear green to human eyes, according to a new study. While for most stars, color is temperature-dependent and limited to a few hues, white dwarfs, which are the dense remnants of sun-like stars that have died, can glow in an incredible range of colors, said lead study author Mark Hollands, an astrophysicist at the University of Warwick, England, on Thursday. “The colors that normal stars can have are pretty much only orange, white or blue,” Hollands told CNN. “What we found is, for most white dwarfs, that’s the same as well. But there are some special cases where the physics in the outer layers of these stars are sufficiently strange that it causes actually quite big deviations in terms of their spectrum,” he said. These deviations are due to the interaction between the helium in their atmosphere and traces of other elements, which vary between white dwarfs, depending on what material has interacted with the star over the course of its lifetime. For instance, iron, magnesium and sodium, elements commonly found in rocks, can be found on the surface — potential evidence of a nearby former planetary system, or from “something like an asteroid that ventures too close to the white dwarf,” Hollands explained. “It gets shredded up into dust, and then those rocky bits of dust and debris fall onto the white dwarf,” he said. “And then that gets mixed into the outer layers, and then you can actually use that to measure what the rocky stuff was made off,” Hollands said. “So we can actually use the white dwarf as a sort of diagnostic tool to actually measure the chemistry of planetary material,” he added. “The white dwarf is taking apart the planets, and we’re able to see what was actually inside that planet — the proportion of the different elements — and that gives us clues in how these planets were formed,” said Adam Burgasser, a professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of California San Diego. “It is a crime scene, and we’re kind of piecing through the evidence that we have left available to us, and that’s allowing us to kind of piece the story of what the planet was and how it was made way, way, way back in in history.” For this study, Hollands looked at the 151 known white dwarf stars that are within 20 parsecs, or around 65 light years, of Earth. As for the green star, the main elements present are calcium, sodium and lithium, Hollands said. “It kind of stimulated interest in me in looking more at that object and why it has so much material being accreted onto it,” said Burgasser, who was not involved in the study. “It can excite the public as well as the scientists in learning more about some of the more, I would say, extreme objects in this sample.” Another notable star was “almost like a salmon pink,” due to the presence of a high density of carbon molecules, Hollands added. While no white dwarf stars can be seen directly from Earth, Hollands was able to calculate their color using star spectrum data, which a statement from the researchers defines as “the ‘fingerprint’ produced when starlight is split apart by wavelength, much like a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow.” Hollands explained that the research has also brought these space objects much closer to home. “It gives you a nice human connection to these very distant things that are so far away that sometimes even as a researcher you feel quite disconnected from these objects that you study,” he said. “But then you can sort of add a human element into it and it feels a lot more tangible.” The observations about the green star are based on existing data and may not shed new understandings about white dwarfs, but the study does offer an intriguing approach and view of these celestial bodies, said Agnès Kim, an astrophysicist and professor of physics at Penn State Scranton, who was not involved in the work. “Doing a study that goes from spectrum to what the human eye would see is a cool intersection of physics and biology to me,” Kim wrote in an email. “I love that some would look green to us if they were close enough for us to see them, and even more fun that some would look pink.” Burgasser added that the study’s categorization scheme using temperatures and atmospheric properties can be useful for the field moving forward. “Some things are kind of purplish pink, and some other things were greenish and blue — and that kind of classification, which by the way we do all the time in astronomy, is classify things, allows us to focus on: why are these types of objects these colors, and are they related to each other based on their composition?” Burgasser said. “We have that information in other forms, but I think this is maybe a simplified way of organizing that data.” Next, Hollands is planning to keep analyzing more white dwarf star spectra, with advances in scientific techniques meaning that researchers will be able to look at a new tranche of stars that are even farther away from Earth. “We know of white dwarfs that we don’t have spectra for,” he said, “but that’s all about to change because there’s quite a few spectroscopic surveys” that are going to start delivering data. “We’ll be getting a tenfold increase in the number of white dwarfs that have spectra,” Hollands said. “And so maybe if we’re lucky, we’ll go from one or maybe two green white dwarfs to 10 or 20.” The study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, or RASTI.

A world with no sunrise still has changing skies, and Webb has caught its water clouds thickening and thinning just 7.5 light-years away. Astronomers have tracked weather on WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, using the James Webb Space Telescope. A team led by Brittany Miles of the University of Arizona’s Steward Observatory watched the Jupiter-sized object for 11 hours, recording a spectrum of its light every 15 minutes. Those observations allowed researchers to distinguish shifting water clouds from gases carried upward by heat deep inside the atmosphere. The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal , provide the most detailed time-series view yet of this frigid neighbor. They also offer the first direct confirmation that water clouds on another world change thickness over time, a familiar feature of weather on Earth. “This is the first time we’ve been able to confirm that water clouds are becoming thinner and thicker on a nearby world,” said Miles, a postdoctoral researcher at Steward Observatory. “Before JWST, we only had photometry, which mixed up the effects of clouds, chemistry, and temperature all together. Now we can actually distinguish them.” Brown dwarfs lack enough mass to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers stars. Instead, they gradually release heat left over from their formation. Although they are generally more massive than planets, the smallest examples make the boundary between the two categories difficult to draw. WISE 0855 sits near that boundary. With roughly twice Jupiter’s mass and almost the same size, it resembles a giant planet traveling through space without a host star. Its temperature is about 265 Kelvin (17 degrees Fahrenheit), below Earth’s average surface temperature. Without a nearby star supplying sunlight, heat escaping from its interior drives atmospheric convection. That gives scientists a chance to examine how a giant world’s own heat shapes its skies. Studying those skies means interpreting light that has passed through layers of clouds and gases. Co-author Mark Marley, director and department head of the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory, compares the challenge to looking through a screen door: researchers must understand both the world beyond it and the filter altering their view. “The photons go through the atmosphere and escape to space,” Marley said. “It’s like looking at the world through a screen door, where the screen is filtering out some of the light. We’re learning about the world on either side of the screen—but we also have to understand the screen itself.” As WISE 0855 rotates, atmospheric regions with different temperatures and cloud coverage come into view. The resulting changes in brightness contain clues about its weather, but brightness alone cannot reveal whether clouds, chemistry, or temperature caused a particular fluctuation. Webb’s medium-resolution spectrograph supplied the missing detail by separating the light into wavelengths associated with individual molecules. Its sensitivity allowed the team to follow changes in specific molecular features on an object too cold and faint for earlier observatories to study this way. The observations revealed high-altitude water clouds becoming thicker and thinner, alongside temperature changes associated with rotation. A separate, repeating wave-like signal appeared in features linked to carbon monoxide and phosphine, pointing to gases transported upward from deeper, hotter layers. That transport resembles the circulation in a heated pot of soup, where warm liquid rises from below. On WISE 0855, convection brings chemicals into cooler atmospheric regions where their abundance differs from what local conditions alone would predict. Scientists call this disequilibrium chemistry. Jupiter’s atmosphere shows the same kind of chemical mixing, and researchers have identified it in other brown dwarfs. What makes these observations different is the ability to follow their variations over time through individual molecules while distinguishing that activity from changes in water clouds. “We’re seeing water clouds getting thicker and thinner, and deep gases rising and falling, and we can actually watch them change in real time,” Miles said. Those connections could help scientists interpret the gas giant exoplanets now coming within Webb’s reach. Worlds can differ greatly in temperature, surroundings, and appearance while sharing the physical processes that move heat, form clouds, and redistribute chemicals. “Even though brown dwarfs are not true planets, they exhibit planet-like behavior,” Miles said. “There is a spectrum of behaviors—not a hard line between brown dwarfs and planets. Jupiter and this object look distinctly different, but they have similar weather patterns. There are basic physics and chemistry that can be applied across all of these worlds.” The study also connects generations of atmospheric research. Miles’s models draw on foundational work by theorists including Marley, whose own models were tested against Jupiter. That groundwork helped the team interpret patterns in Webb’s observations. “A lot of my physical intuition on what is missing from the models is because of Mark’s mentorship and hard work,” she said. “This is a multi-year project. A lot of people contributed to make sure this could be done right.” Miles now wants longer Webb observations to better establish WISE 0855’s rotation and investigate the three-dimensional movement of its atmosphere. Reference: “Water Cloud and Chemical Modulations in the Coldest Brown Dwarf” by Brittany E. Miles, James Mang, Caroline V. Morley, Andrew J. I. Skemer, Melanie Rowland, Brianna Lacy, Genaro Suarez, Channon Visscher, Dániel Apai, Gordon Bjoraker, Aarynn L. Carter, Jacqueline K. Faherty, Jonathan J. Fortney, Nguyen Fuda, Thomas Geballe, Harshil Kothari, Mary Anne Limbach, Mark Marley, Allison M. McCarthy, Adam Schneider, Johanna Vos, Michael Cushing, Richard Freedman, Michael Line, Roxana Lupu, Emily Martin and Mikayla J. Wilson, September 16, 2026, arXiv .
